title: Traditional Pearl Diving Practices off the Coast of Bahrain

paragraphs.text: For hundreds of years, pearls originating from the Arabian Gulf have been recognised as some of the world's finest gemstones. In the mid-1800s, many of the inhabitants of the surrounding lands were in some way connected to the local pearl industry, but the core of this industry was located on the island of Bahrain. In 'The Book of the Pearl', G.F. Kunz tells us that in 1908, fisheries in the area employed about 3,500 boats, large and small, of which 1,200 would sail out of Bahrain.

A typical crew on a Bahraini boat, known as a Dhow or Sambuk, that fished for pearl oysters consisted of many people. The captain was an expert fisherman with knowledge of all waters and the best pearling banks, and was, in general, the owner of the boat. The second-in-command was responsible for ensuring that orders given by the captain were obeyed. Other crew members included the Al-Musally, who was a prayer leader, and the Nahham, who was in charge of songs to keep the crew's spirits up and to bring luck. The topman stayed on the boat monitoring the progress and safety of the diver, while the deckhand performed all manner of tasks at the request of other crew members. Finally, there was the Ghawwas or pearl diver.

The life of a Bahraini pearl diver was harsh. During the pearling season, which was between April and September, they had to leave their families behind while they went away to dive. Even if the diving season was fruitful and the harvest high, the divers still had to endure the next half a year without pay until the diving season started again.

The entire crew's existence on board was simple, to say the least; living off a diet of dates, fish, rice and coffee. However, it was the divers who suffered most; aside from overexertion and malnourishment, they faced the daily threat of being hunted and severely wounded by sharks, and of developing long-term neural problems caused by insufficient supplies of oxygen during prolonged periods of time underwater.

The diving methods employed on these boats remained basic, unchanged since diving for pearls had first started. Once anchored near the oyster beds, everything revolved around the diver and his topman. The diver would sink to the bottom, helped by a thick rope tied to a stone. Then, the topman literally held the diver's life in his hands, for if he did not pull the diver up fast enough, the diver would drown. The divers worked in fifteen-minute shifts, and in that time made at least eight visits to the sea bed nine to twelve metres down.

Typically, divers would put on a nose clip, leather gloves to guard against sharp coral, and wear a net basket around their neck. After the divers resurfaced, the oysters were piled on deck, left to dry in the sun and then opened; whether or not the oysters contained pearls was a matter of pure chance. Up to a whole week could go by, and thousands of oysters could pass through the crew's hands without a single pearl being found. Then again, a few hours of diving could result in a very profitable supply. Whenever and however they came to the surface, the pearls always ended up in the captain's red cloth pouch.

The captain would sell his pearl harvest to the local pearl dealer, who would board the boat when it returned to the harbour. Here the dealer would examine and purchase the pearls and then resell to bigger merchants. Once the captain had received the money, he paid each crew member according to their rank in the hierarchy, the largest share going to himself.

Arabian dialects used in this region include a variety of words for pearl: Lulu, Dana, Hussah, Gumashah. Then there are the names to describe a pearl's shape and colour: Sujani, pear-shaped drop, Khazli, high-domed upper half with a half-rounded bottom; Adasi, rounded shaped drop; Majhoolah, a large, ugly pearl that can conceal a finer pearl cylinder with flat sides, and Majhoolah, a large, ugly pearl that can conceal a finer pearl inside. Extraordinary expertise and patience were needed to remove the thin layers of a Majhoolah, a process that could take weeks. Of all the pearls, the one that a crew hoped to see was the Jiwan, meaning young, which was the perfect white rose-tinted, round pearl that radiated light and beauty. Pearls from the waters around Bahrain were, and still are to this day, sorted and graded using a sequence of sieves called Gurbal. Pearls are weighed using an ancient complex unit of weight called a Chow; one carat equals 0.6518 Chow.

The buying of pearls sometimes revolved around a particular method of bidding, where a dealer who wished to conceal from others the price he was negotiating would cover his and his client's clasped hands with a cloth and then use a system of finger signals. From Bahrain, the pearls were sold to Indian merchants, who sent them to Bombay, where they were drilled by hand. From there the pearls were sold to Europeans, whose thirst for these pearls in the 1800s was unquenchable.
